Concurrent medical conditions included sinusitis, allergic rhinitis, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, bipolar disorder, asthma (Mild persistent ) and obesity. Concomitant products included paliperidone (Invega).   On 13th February 2009, the patient received the 1st dose of Boostrix (intramuscular) and the 1st dose of MENACTRA (intramuscular). On 13th February 2009, less than a day after receiving Boostrix, the patient experienced arthus reaction (serious criteria GSK medically significant), injection site erythema, palpitation, red rash and tenderness. On an unknown date, the outcome of the arthus reaction, injection site erythema, palpitation, red rash and tenderness were unknown.   The reporter considered the arthus reaction, injection site erythema, palpitation, red rash and tenderness to be related to Boostrix.  Additional details were provided as follows: This case was reported in a literature article and described the occurrence of erythema in shot area, arthus reaction in an 11-year-old male patient, who was vaccinated with BOOSTRIX (GLAXOSMITHKLINE) for prophylaxis. The VAERS ID was 340381. The patient was a part of the study that aimed to describe trends in spontaneously reported Arthus reactions following tetanus toxoid, reduced diphtheria toxoid, and acellular pertussis vaccines (Tdap) and to assess the risk of this phenomenon in persons receiving Tdap repeatedly. The goal of this literature review was to identify published studies of Tdap vaccines administered in adolescents and adults who received a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine less than or equal to 5 years previously. [It was reviewed Arthus reports in the Vaccine Adverse Events Reporting System (VAERS), 1990-2018. A systematic literature review was conducted for any Arthus cases reported in Tdap clinical trials and observational studies published between 2000 and 2019. Of the total of 619,479 reports in VAERS, it was identified 192 records coded with the "Type III immune complex mediated reaction" term. All but one had vaccination dates between 2000 and 2018. The reports mentioned 35 different vaccines administered alone or coadministered in various combinations. The most frequently reported vaccine types, i.e., mentioned in more than 10 reports, were inactivated influenza vaccine (n = 39), pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (n = 39), Tdap (n = 36), measles mumps rubella (n = 20), inactivated polio vaccine (n = 17), Td (n = 16), hepatitis A vaccine (n = 14), meningococcal conjugate vaccine (n = 14), and varicella vaccine (n = 14). 36 (thirty-six) reports mentioning Tdap were received between 2006 and 2018. The Vaccine Adverse Events Reporting System (VAERS) received spontaneous reports of adverse events after vaccination from healthcare providers, patients, parents, vaccine manufacturers, and others. It was searched for the preferred term "Type III immune complex mediated reaction" in reports submitted to VAERS between 11 June 1990 (the start of VAERS system database) and 14 December 2018]. The patient had no lab data. The patient's current illness included sinusitis and allergic rhinitis. The patient's preexisting conditions included INVEGA; crab meat; medical conditions showed ADHD; Bipolar disorder, DDD, Mild persistent asthma; Obesity; Allergic rhinitis. No information on patient's family history, or concomitant medication was provided. On 13 February 2009, the patient received 1st dose of BOOSTRIX (TDAP/ GLAXOSMITHKLINE BIOLOGICALS) vaccine (Site: UN/ Route: IM; Lot: AC52B029AA); 1st dose of MENACTRA (MNQ: meningococcal conjugate/ SANOFI PASTEUR) (Site: UN/ Route: IM; Lot: U2666AA). [Tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines included pediatric diphtheria and tetanus toxoids vaccine (DT), tetanus toxoid vaccine (Ttox), adult tetanus toxoid reduced diphtheria toxoid vaccine (Td), and Tdap. Tdap was administered alone in 22 of these cases. In 14 persons it was coadministered with other vaccines, such as inactivated influenza, hepatitis B, hepatitis A, human papilloma virus, meningococcal conjugate, measles-mumps-rubella, and pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines]. On 13 February 2009, the patient's mother stated erythema in shot area started day of injection, worsened through weekend. Presented to Clinic 16 February 2009 with large (about 10 × 11 cm) erythematous area on left upper arm, mildly tender to palpation, no fevers, no induration. The patient was diagnosed with arthus reaction. [PT terms: Injection site erythema, Palpitations, Rash erythematous, Tenderness, Type III immune complex mediated reaction]. [Most reports provided very limited information on the clinical course and laboratory workup. There were no cases of severe sequelae, such as skin necrosis. One report represented a literature case of erythema nodosum in temporal association with Tdap vaccination (VAERS captures cases and case-series of adverse events published in the literature as spontaneous reports). Arthus reaction was mentioned in the manuscript as one of several differential diagnoses (the final diagnosis being vaccine-associated erythema nodosum). No reports mentioned the use of Tdap during pregnancy. Between 2011 and 2018, approximately 169,000,000 doses of Tdap vaccines were distributed. During the same time, 24 presumed Arthus reaction cases following Tdap were reported to VAERS, for an estimated reporting rate of 0.1 per million doses distributed]. Treatment was unknown. The patient was not recovered. The patient had ER visit. The author commented, "Since the 1980s, literature reports and reviews of Arthus reaction following tetanus-containing vaccines have become rare. This is probably due to a wider acceptance by vaccine providers of the general recommendation not to re-administer tetanus vaccines more frequently than every 10 years. Other factors are undoubtedly improvements in standardization and purity of modern tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines. In this review, we found that the risk of Arthus reactions following vaccines used in the past two decades is extremely low. Only 36 reports were found in the VAERS database following Tdap booster. Several studies identified in our literature review support the idea that Tdap vaccines do not noticeably increase the risk of injection site reactions, when administered following a recent dose of tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine. The safety of multiple doses of Tdap vaccine administered in pregnant women was evaluated in a retrospective large database study. Cases were reported after a wide variety of pediatric and adult vaccines. Most reactions reported were mild and self-limiting without treatment. The review confirmed that overall incidence of Arthus reactions was very low. No information related to Tdap vaccine was presented in the review. The authors stressed the need for the standard definition and diagnostic criteria of the reaction. Arthus reaction following vaccination is difficult to study, because of its rarity. The prescribing information documents for all tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines used provide a warning about the use of these products in persons who have experienced an Arthus-type hypersensitivity following a prior dose of a tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine. They state that such persons usually have a high level of tetanus antitoxin and that they should not receive tetanus toxoid-containing vaccines unless at least 10 years have elapsed since the last dose. Providers who suspect an Arthus reaction in adult patients receiving a tetanus toxoid- containing vaccine, including Tdap, should consider serology testing for tetanus and diphtheria antibodies. Very high concentrations measured in the patient's blood within a few days after vaccination would support the diagnosis. Other conditions and reactions that may present similar symptoms and complaints (e.g., sterile abscess, cellulitis, SIRVA, etc.) may need to be ruled out. Accurate diagnosis and confirmation of Arthus reaction is important, and, ideally, it should be a histological diagnosis with demonstration of a vasculitis. Confusing an expected injection site reaction (not Type III hypersensitivity) for Arthus reaction with the subsequent recommendation to avoid tetanus or diphtheria toxoid-containing vaccines may have negative consequences for the individual. Limitations of our study include those inherent to passive surveillance systems, such as VAERS, including over- or underreporting, biased reporting, inconsistency in quality and completeness of reports, and, in general, inability to assess the causality." The author concluded, "In conclusion, the risk of Arthus reaction following Tdap vaccine administration appears to be extremely low. This should provide reassurance to vaccine providers considering the increasing use of Tdap vaccines in the adult population, including in pregnant women. Future research into Arthus reaction following immunization would benefit from the development of a standard case-definition." Abstract:  Since the last review of vaccine safety surveillance data for erythema multiforme (EM), Stevens Johnson syndrome (SJS), SJS/TEN, and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) (EM/SJS/TEN), over 37 new vaccines have been introduced. We sought to describe reported EM/SJS/TEN after vaccines during 1999-2017. Methods: We identified reports of EM/SJS/TEN received by the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) during 1999-2017. We stratified analysis by condition (EM, SJS, or TEN), and analyzed reports by serious or non-serious status, sex, age group, time from vaccination to symptom onset, exposure to known causes of EM/SJS/TEN, and vaccines administered. We used data mining to detect vaccine-AE pairs reported more frequently than expected. Results: Of 466,027 reports to VAERS during 1999-017, we identified 984 reports of EM, 89 reports of SJS, 6 reports of SJS/TEN, and 7 reports of TEN. Few reports of EM (9%), and most reports of SJS (52%), SJS/TEN (100%), and TEN (100%) were serious. Overall, 55% of reports described males, 48% described children aged 4 years; 58% of EM/SJS/TEN occurred 7 days after vaccination. Few reports (5%) described exposure to known causes of EM/SJS/TEN. Overall, childhood vaccines (e.g., combined measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine) were most commonly reported. We identified 6 deaths; 4 were exposed to medications associated with EM/SJS/TEN. EM after smallpox vaccine was reported disproportionately among people aged 19 - 49 years. Conclusions: EM/SJS/TEN were rarely reported after vaccination; data mining identified a known association between EM and smallpox vaccine. He was initially alert and oriented, febrile and tachycardic. Laboratory data failed to reveal any abnormalities on a toxicology screen but was notable for an elevated serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK) and lactate, 204 U/L and 9.2 mmol/L, respectively. A review of his medical record revealed vaccination for smallpox 8 days prior to presentation. Supportive therapy failed to prevent the patient from developing disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with rapidly upward trending liver enzymes. CPK level and urinalysis demonstrated myoglobunirua. He progressed to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome with hepatic encephalopathy and acute kidney injury requiring dialysis. On hospital day five he became hypotensive and developed a fatal arrhythmia. Autopsy revealed a dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with histologic evidence of myocarditis, a necrotic liver, an infarcted right adrenal gland and an edematous brain with patchy areas of acute neuronal necrosis directly attributed to immunologic consequences of the smallpox vaccine. Discussion: To our knowledge, this is the first case of death from the smallpox vaccine in a young, healthy, active person. Myocarditis is well-reported; however, in this pt. myocarditis silently progressed to DCM as a result of a systemic immunologic response to the vaccine. The same immunologic response coupled with exertion which occurred post-vaccine day 8, the peak of expected response to vaccine, likely led to his multi-organ system failure and death. Continuous vigilance for adverse reactions to smallpox vaccine is warranted."
